hypothesis: There is NO published, controlled measurement establishing the gas/dispatch overhead of a Weiroll-class on-chain scripting interpreter (assembly + mcopy return-data chaining) relative to either equivalent hand-written multi-call sequences or to native batching such as Multicall3. The widely-repeated claim that such interpreters are 'gas-efficient' is, in the corpus, an unmeasured design assertion rather than an empirical effect.
rationale: The only corpus paper describing this exact artifact class, 'MultiCall: A Transaction-batching Interpreter for Ethereum' (2021), carries only ~2 citations and provides no abstract or reported gas benchmark in the corpus, so no quantitative dispatch-overhead figure is on record. The VM-performance papers that do measure execution cost study the wrong layer: 'VM Matters: A Comparison of WASM VMs and EVMs in the Performance of Blockchain Smart Contracts' compares whole-VM engines (WASM vs EVM), 'A Performance Survey on Stack-based and Register-based Virtual Machines' is a generic non-blockchain VM-architecture study, and 'A Metric-Based Approach to Modelling a Virtual Machine for Smart Contract Execution' models a VM abstractly without benchmarking an interpreter-dispatch layer against a baseline. Gas-cost work in the corpus ('Gas Estimation and Optimization for Smart Contracts on Ethereum', 'GASOL: Gas Analysis and Optimization for Ethereum Smart Contracts', 'A Max-SMT Superoptimizer for EVM handling Memory and Storage', 'Inferring Needless Write Memory Accesses on Ethereum Bytecode') optimizes ordinary contract bytecode, never the per-call interpretive dispatch + memory-copy cost of a batching scripting VM. The corpus is therefore silent on whether the interpreter overhead is small, negligible, or net-negative versus simply issuing the calls directly.
supports_if: A study reports head-to-head gas measurements of a Weiroll/MultiCall-class interpreter executing N chained calls versus (a) the same calls issued as separate EOA transactions, (b) a hand-written aggregator, and (c) Multicall3-style batching, across varied call counts and return-data sizes, showing the interpreter's dispatch + mcopy overhead is bounded and characterized (e.g., constant per-call gas with a stated coefficient). The effect IS real if any corpus-grade source quantifies the overhead and shows the efficiency claim holds.
refutes_if: No corpus paper provides such a controlled gas comparison; the 'gas-efficient' claim remains supported only by design narrative (MultiCall 2021) or by VM-level comparisons that do not isolate the scripting-interpreter dispatch layer. Finding that all gas measurements in the corpus target contract bytecode optimization or whole-VM engine comparison, not the interpreter overhead of a batching scripting VM, confirms the absence.
motivating_papers: MultiCall: A Transaction-batching Interpreter for Ethereum
VM Matters: A Comparison of WASM VMs and EVMs in the Performance of Blockchain Smart Contracts
A Performance Survey on Stack-based and Register-based Virtual Machines
A Metric-Based Approach to Modelling a Virtual Machine for Smart Contract Execution
Gas Estimation and Optimization for Smart Contracts on Ethereum
A Max-SMT Superoptimizer for EVM handling Memory and Storage

hypothesis: Formal verification of an on-chain transaction-scripting interpreter has NOT been done, and there is NO evidence that applying formal methods to such an interpreter (its dispatch loop, offset/bit-field decoding, and memory-copy semantics) yields any measurable real-world bug reduction. The corpus's large formal-verification literature targets contract/bytecode safety in general and never the scripting-VM dispatch layer, so the assumed verifiability benefit for this artifact class is unsubstantiated.
rationale: The corpus contains an extensive formal-methods body, but every instance targets either contract semantics or the base EVM, not a batching-interpreter dispatch layer: 'KEVM: A Complete Semantics of the Ethereum Virtual Machine', 'eThor: Practical and Provably Sound Static Analysis of Ethereum Smart Contracts', 'HoRStify: Sound Security Analysis of Smart Contracts', 'VerX: Safety Verification of Smart Contracts', 'solc-verify: A Modular Verifier for Solidity Smart Contracts', 'Formally Verified EVM Block-Optimizations', 'EVM-Vale: Formal Verification of EVM Bytecode Using Vale', 'Formal and Executable Semantics of the Ethereum Virtual Machine in Dafny', and 'An Operational Semantics for Yul' all verify general contracts or the EVM/Yul, none verifies an interpreter that decodes packed offset descriptors and chains return data via mcopy. Moreover, none of the surveys ('A Survey on Security Verification of Blockchain Smart Contracts', 'Formal Methods for the Verification of Smart Contracts: A Review', 'Smart Contracts Formal Verification: A Systematic Literature Review') reports a controlled study linking formal verification to a measured reduction in exploited bugs in deployed code; the benefit is asserted programmatically (e.g., 'Advancing Blockchain Security: The Imperative of Formal Verification ... Editorial') rather than demonstrated empirically. The custom bit-packed offset encoding that defines this artifact class (40-bit memTargets, 16-bit lengths, mcopy regions) has no semantic formalization in the corpus at all.
supports_if: A paper formalizes a transaction-batching scripting interpreter's dispatch and memory model (including the offset bit-field decoding and mcopy return-data chaining) and proves memory-safety / no-overlap / faithful-chaining properties; AND/OR an empirical study shows formally verified interpreters or contracts exhibit a statistically significant lower exploited-bug rate than unverified equivalents. Either would make the verifiability benefit a real, measured effect.
refutes_if: No corpus paper formalizes a scripting-interpreter dispatch/memory layer, and no corpus paper provides a measured bug-reduction comparison (verified vs unverified) for any EVM artifact; all formal-verification entries either target general contracts/EVM or assert benefits without outcome measurement. This confirms the effect is currently unproven for this artifact class.
motivating_papers: KEVM: A Complete Semantics of the Ethereum Virtual Machine
eThor: Practical and Provably Sound Static Analysis of Ethereum Smart Contracts
HoRStify: Sound Security Analysis of Smart Contracts
Formal Methods for the Verification of Smart Contracts: A Review
Advancing Blockchain Security: The Imperative of Formal Verification for Smart Contracts Editorial

hypothesis: The literature does NOT formally characterize the gas-vs-expressiveness-vs-verifiability trade-off for on-chain scripting VMs as a coupled design space; in particular there is NO evidence that gains in interpreter expressiveness/composability (chained return data, dynamic offsets) trade off against gas or verifiability in any measured or proven way. 'Composability' in the corpus is an economic/protocol-integration construct, disconnected from the interpreter-design properties the research question poses.
rationale: The corpus treats the three axes in entirely separate, non-overlapping silos, and never as a joint trade-off for a scripting interpreter. Composability papers operate at the protocol/economic level, not the VM-expressiveness level: 'Measuring Asset Composability as a Proxy for DeFi Integration', 'Formal Analysis of Composable DeFi Protocols', 'DeFi Composability as MEV Non-interference' / 'DeFi composability as MEV non-interference', and 'Where do DeFi stablecoins go? A closer look at what DeFi composability really means' define composability via cross-protocol asset flows and MEV/non-interference, never via an interpreter's ability to chain return data within one atomic transaction. The single interpreter paper ('MultiCall: A Transaction-batching Interpreter for Ethereum') is not cited alongside any composability or verification paper and offers no expressiveness metric. No corpus paper presents a Pareto analysis, an impossibility result, or even paired measurements showing that adding expressive features (e.g., partial return-data chaining) costs gas or impairs verifiability. The trade-off framing in the research question is therefore a hypothesis the corpus neither confirms nor quantifies; the apparent 'trade-off' may be an artifact of conflating distinct literatures that never measured the same system.
supports_if: A study (or set of comparable studies on one system) jointly measures or formally relates interpreter expressiveness (number/kind of chainable operations), gas cost, and verification effort/coverage for a scripting VM, demonstrating a quantified trade-off curve or a proven impossibility/tension among the three axes. Connecting interpreter-level expressiveness to a composability metric and to a gas or verifiability cost would make the trade-off a real, characterized effect.
refutes_if: Composability remains defined only economically/at protocol scope, formal-verification work remains scoped to contract/EVM safety, and gas work remains scoped to bytecode optimization, with no paper measuring or proving relationships among expressiveness, gas, and verifiability for a single scripting interpreter. The absence of any joint characterization confirms the trade-off is, in this corpus, unestablished.
